summary: The developer machine has the core runtimes (Node 24, npm/npx), Docker and az CLI signed-in, and the run-environment declares DOCUMENTDB_URI and the target database name, so a Node.js sample can be implemented and run against the provided live Azure DocumentDB cluster. However no DocumentDB-specific agent skills or MCP servers are installed, several CLI helpers (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are missing, and many service-specific facts from the cold answers could not be verified from on-machine documentation or skills; several knowledge gaps (embedding dims, exact vector-index creation syntax, recommended driver pinning, notification transport, LLM choice) remain and must be resolved by the builder before or during the build. Workarounds exist for many missing tools (npm-install packages, use az for control-plane inspection, use Docker or the live cluster for data-plane checks), so the build can start but with caution and extra manual steps.
summary_points: Core OS toolchain present: node (v24), npx, npm (via node), git, docker and az CLI (signed in); DOCUMENTDB_URI and database name are provided in the run environment text, so data-plane connectivity is expected.
No DocumentDB agent skills or MCP servers are installed (DocumentDB MCP Toolkit, DocumentDB Agent Kit, Learn MCP server absent) — these accelerators would save time and are missing.
Key CLIs for interactive DB work (mongosh) and IaC (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are not on PATH; they are recommended but not strictly blocking for this sample.

Many cold-answer quiz items about Azure DocumentDB control-plane resource names, CLI groups, connection-string format, auth options, and exact vector-index commands could not be verified from on-machine docs/skills and need authoritative doc links or installation of the Learn/DocumentDB MCP servers.

Builder can proceed using the live cluster and standard Node MongoDB driver (npm install mongodb), but must decide LLM/embedding provider, embedding dims, exact index creation syntax, and notification mechanism before finalizing code and index parameters.
Run-policy forbids Azure control-plane writes (azure_writes_allowed: false) so do not attempt to provision new clusters; the sample should operate against the existing cluster only.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB account resource).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: No on-machine Learn/MCP documentation or skill present to confirm the current control-plane resource provider naming; Microsoft historically used Microsoft.DocumentDB for Cosmos DB which causes overlap.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the wrong provider/resource type when authoring IaC or az commands, control-plane operations would fail; however the sample is meant to run against an existing cluster so exact control-plane resource type is not strictly needed unless adding IaC.
improvements: Add an authoritative learn.microsoft.com link or an MCP server entry (Learn MCP Server) to the agent kit so the agent can resolve the current resource provider and resource type automatically.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name MyAccount --resource-group MyRg --locations regionName=eastus ...
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer matches the Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) CLI experience; without the Learn MCP Server or docs on-machine we cannot confirm whether the managed 'Azure DocumentDB' service uses the same az group or a service-specific extension.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands when the service expects a different command group or extension could cause failed CLI commands or attempts to manage the wrong resource type.
improvements: Add quickstart docs or an MCP lookup so an agent can confirm the current CLI command group (az cosmosdb vs az documentdb extension) before generating commands.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: These resource names match Azure Cosmos DB historically; without on-machine docs the agent can't confirm whether the managed DocumentDB offering uses the same ARM resource or a new resource type.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder authored IaC for the wrong resource type the templates would fail; since run_policy forbids control-plane writes and the sample uses an existing cluster, this is low immediate risk but matters if IaC is later added.
improvements: Expose an MCP server or a Learn quickstart snippet so the agent can verify the correct ARM/Terraform resource types.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Cosmos DB Mongo API: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000 (or tls=true).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The string shown matches Azure Cosmos DB's Mongo API format; the managed 'Azure DocumentDB' offering may use a different host suffix/port or TLS parameters. No on-machine docs to confirm exact connection string syntax required by this product.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder hardcodes the cosmos-style host suffix and port, the MongoDB driver may not connect to this managed service; the sample must read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env and not attempt to construct the connection string.
improvements: Add a canonical connection-string example to the agent kit README and the run-environment skill so builders do not reuse Cosmos DB-specific strings incorrectly.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB is billed in Request Units (RUs); choose provisioned throughput (RU/s) or serverless.
confusions.grounded_answer: The run-environment indicates the target cluster uses a compute tier (example: 'compute tier M30') and is vector-capable, so this managed Azure DocumentDB offering uses compute tiers (vCore-like tiers), not request-unit-based billing.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer describes Azure Cosmos DB (MongoDB API) RU-based billing; the provided run-environment explicitly states compute tier M30 for the DocumentDB cluster, indicating a vCore/compute-tier billing model.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RUs they might create indexes and queries tuned for RU billing and attempt to use control-plane commands that only apply to Cosmos DB; index sizing/throughput decisions could be misconfigured.
improvements: Add an explicit sentence in the run-environment README and in the agent kit stating the billing model (compute-tier M-series) so builders do not assume RUs.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB API: use MongoDB username/password (account key); Entra ID/Azure AD integration is not generally supported for the MongoDB API.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflects Cosmos DB historical behavior; we lack on-machine docs or skills that confirm whether Azure DocumentDB supports Entra ID or other auth flows for the MongoDB-compatible endpoint.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Entra ID support when it's not available, authentication will fail; conversely, assuming only key-based auth if AD auth is supported will miss better security options.
improvements: Include an authentication summary in the agent kit or run-environment skill specifying supported authentication mechanisms and examples (connection string vs. AD token).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., official Node.js 'mongodb' package).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the official MongoDB Node.js driver (mongodb) from npm; prefer the MongoDB-compatible driver rather than Cosmos DB-specific SDKs for MongoDB workloads.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the prompt review recommended the official 'mongodb' package for Node.
confusions.build_risk: Low if followed; using the wrong SDK (Cosmos SQL SDK) would cause incompatibility.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports HNSW, IVF and DiskANN; example: createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine' }).
confusions.grounded_answer: The run-environment explicitly says the cluster is 'vector-capable' and lists DiskANN, HNSW and IVF as available index types; however the exact createIndex syntax and option names were not present on-machine and so cannot be verified.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer correctly named the index types (matches skill_md) but proposed a createIndex syntax whose option names (vectorIndexType, dims, distance) may be implementation-specific and were not confirmed.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the example createIndex options verbatim, index creation may fail due to mismatched option names or required commands; index creation should be implemented via driver APIs validated against the cluster.
improvements: Document the precise createIndex call and option names in the agent kit or a Learn quickstart; include an example Node script to create an HNSW index with the correct option names.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for full-text/hybrid vector+text search; the MongoDB API itself does not provide a hybrid search engine on the Azure control plane.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer describes a common Cosmos+Search integration pattern; we have no on-machine docs confirming whether this managed DocumentDB offering has built-in hybrid search or expects Azure Cognitive Search integration.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes hybrid vector+text search is available natively when it isn't, the alert/query design will fail; conversely, overcomplicating by integrating external Azure Cognitive Search when the cluster supports built-in hybrid search is unnecessary.
improvements: Add a short 'search capabilities' section to the agent kit clarifying whether hybrid vector+text search is supported natively and giving the recommended integration pattern.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB lagged; supported wire proto versions may be older and some features (server-side JS, some admin commands, change streams) may be limited.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer summarizes historical Cosmos DB behavior; we have no on-machine doc to confirm which wire-version this managed DocumentDB cluster advertises (skill_md mentioned 'MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol' in the run-environment description, but that was in the top-level skill_md text and not repeated in the cold answer list).
confusions.build_risk: Using unsupported features or relying on change streams could cause runtime failures; the builder must test target commands against the live cluster.
improvements: Provide an MCP lookup or a quickstart snippet showing the exact supported MongoDB wire protocol/server version and a short list of unsupported features.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: No full-featured emulator; run official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:6/7) on port 27017. For true Cosmos DB compatibility you must run against live Azure account.
confusions.grounding_source: Known accelerators list (Local DocumentDB container) and Run environment (skill_md)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer is correct that mongo:6 is an option for generic Mongo development, but the provided known_accelerators show an open-source DocumentDB engine and a Local DocumentDB container option that is intended to emulate the managed service more closely; that alternative was not noted in the cold answer.
confusions.build_risk: Using mongo:6 for local dev may miss compatibility nuances with the DocumentDB engine; prefer running the DocumentDB open-source image if exact behavior matching is needed.
improvements: Document the recommended local image (open-source DocumentDB) and provide a docker run command in the agent kit and run-environment notes.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change Streams support historically limited/unavailable; Cosmos DB offers a change feed on the SQL API.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer reflects Cosmos DB historical behavior; no on-machine docs confirm whether this Azure DocumentDB offering supports MongoDB change streams or whether change-stream-like behavior requires another API.
confusions.build_risk: If the alert agent relies on MongoDB change streams and the service lacks them, real-time alerting will not work; builder should use polling, a processed flag, the change feed (if available), or a supported mechanism.
improvements: Add a short compatibility section in the agent kit specifying whether MongoDB change streams are supported and example alternatives if they are not.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: There isn't a separate service-specific MCP server known; use Azure management MCP and standard MongoDB tools.
confusions.grounded_answer: The known accelerators list includes an 'Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit' (data-plane tools) and also the general Azure MCP Server and Microsoft Learn MCP Server; those accelerators are not installed on the machine but they exist and would provide the specialized tooling.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer missed the documented accelerators on-machine; there is a service-specific MCP Toolkit available per the known accelerators table.
confusions.build_risk: Missing specialized MCP tooling slows development and increases the chance of index/command mistakes; index creation and schema inspection will need manual driver scripts or mongosh.
improvements: Install or reference the Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit in the agent kit and provide an 'mcp.json' entry so an agent can start the appropriate MCP server automatically.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically 'DocumentDB' referred to the original SQL-document API and later became Azure Cosmos DB; the MongoDB-compatible offering is the Cosmos DB API for MongoDB and unrelated to the open-source DocumentDB project.
confusions.grounding_source: Developer briefing (task instructions) and Run environment (skill_md)
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Naming has shifted historically (DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB) and similar names are used across different Microsoft products; the cold answer conflates general DocumentDB history with the current managed 'Azure DocumentDB' product identity.
confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion can lead builders to follow the wrong docs (Cosmos DB docs vs the new product docs) and choose incorrect CLI commands or SDKs.
improvements: Add a short 'Terminology and history' section to the agent kit and run-environment README clarifying the current product name, its relation to Cosmos DB APIs, and the open-source DocumentDB project.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The service uses Cosmos DB's own engine and presents a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol; application code should use MongoDB drivers but be aware of some behavioral differences.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer repeats the common Cosmos DB characterization; without on-machine docs we can't assert whether this managed DocumentDB's engine is the same or if it changes any application behavior in specific ways.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes exact parity with MongoDB server semantics they may call unsupported commands; must test against the live cluster.
improvements: Provide an engine-compatibility summary in the agent kit with a short list of unsupported commands and recommended workarounds.

confusions.question: What database and collection names will this sample use and what environment variable holds the connection string?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name sample_fintech_11. Read connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not persist the real URI in files.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use database 'sample_fintech_11' and read the cluster connection string at runtime from environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI; put a placeholder in .env.example and do not commit real credentials.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: N/A — the run-environment explicitly states these details.
confusions.build_risk: Low if followed; storing real credentials in repo would be a security risk.

confusions.question: What Node.js client package and connect call will the sample use to open a connection?
confusions.cold_answer: Use official mongodb driver: const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb'); const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }); await client.connect();
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the official mongodb Node.js driver and connect with MongoClient using DOCUMENTDB_URI; pick recent stable driver options appropriate for Node 24 and MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Prompt review recommended the mongodb package; builder must pick the exact version to match wire protocol support.
confusions.build_risk: If driver version is incompatible with the cluster's wire protocol (e.g., driver too old/new), connections or features may fail; pin a driver version that supports MongoDB 7.0.
improvements: Add a recommended package.json snippet to the agent kit specifying a tested mongodb driver major (e.g., 'mongodb': '^5.7.0' or later) and a note to validate against the target wire protocol.

confusions.question: What document shape and index will be used to store scraped news with embeddings so the agents can query efficiently?
confusions.cold_answer: Document: { _id, headline, url, publishedAt, tickers, sentiment, embedding } with a text index on headline and a vector index on embedding: createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', dims: 1536, distance: 'cosine' }).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Run environment confirms vector-capable cluster exists but does not state the exact index creation API option names nor the embedding dimensionality (depends on embedding model chosen).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder chooses dims that don't match the embedding model or uses incorrect index options, index creation will fail and similarity queries will be wrong.
improvements: Document a recommended document schema and provide a concrete Node.js index-creation script with the exact option names tested against the cluster.

confusions.question: How will the alert agent check for watchlist matches efficiently?
confusions.cold_answer: Query by publishedAt/flag and match tickers via db.articles.find({ tickers: { $in: watchlist } }). For fuzzy text+vector matching, run a vector nearest-neighbor query constrained by text filters if the service supports hybrid queries.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The basic ticker-matching using $in is correct and safe; the availability of hybrid vector+filter queries is product-specific and was not confirmed on-machine.
confusions.build_risk: If hybrid queries are not supported the builder must implement separate steps (filter then vector search or vector search then filter) which will change performance characteristics.
improvements: Add a tested example in the agent kit demonstrating the recommended pattern for combining text/attribute filters with vector nearest-neighbor queries on the DocumentDB cluster.

confusions.question: What permissions and authentication does the sample expect when connecting to the cluster from the developer machine?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample expects a full-privilege connection string (primary key style) in DOCUMENTDB_URI so it can create the sample database/collections and indexes; it will not attempt Entra ID.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use a full-privilege connection string provided in DOCUMENTDB_URI (as declared in the run-environment) and operate only within sample_fintech_11; do not use Entra ID unless the builder elects and documents that flow.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Run environment explicitly stated DOCUMENTDB_URI and that the sample will create collections/indexes within sample_fintech_11.
confusions.build_risk: If the provided URI lacks sufficient privileges the sample may fail to create collections/indexes; verify the connection string has required permissions before running seed scripts.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the DocumentDB connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and never hardcode a host suffix or port; the run-environment declares this env var as authoritative.

Use the official Node.js 'mongodb' driver to connect (MongoClient) and pin a recent driver version that supports MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol; test connection against the live cluster before creating indexes.
Do not assume request-unit (RU) billing or Cosmos DB-specific control-plane behavior — this cluster is described as compute-tier M30; design index and throughput choices for compute-tier billing.

Do not rely on hybrid vector+filter queries until you verify the exact vector-index API on the cluster; implement alert logic that can fall back to filtering by tickers ($in) and then run a vector search in a second step if needed.
